title: FreQuency
subtitle: Build the song while moving through it
summary: FreQuency is Harmonix's PlayStation 2 rhythm game, released in North America on 20 November 2001. body: FreQuency is Harmonix's PlayStation 2 rhythm game, released in North America on 20 November 2001. The player travels through an octagonal tunnel whose walls carry the separate parts of a song. Drums, bass, vocals and other layers appear as sequences of notes to perform with the controller. Playing a section correctly brings that musical part into the mix. Instead of treating a complete recording as an untouched backing track, the game asks the player to assemble its sound while moving through the tunnel.

Completing two measures of a track without an error captures it, allowing that part to continue automatically until a later section. The player can then rotate to another wall and work on the next instrument. Good play fills the song out; repeated mistakes reduce the energy meter and can end the attempt. The tunnel makes those choices visible as neighbouring lanes, so reading the music also means choosing where to go next. Special items can capture a part immediately or increase the points earned.

The track list draws on different contemporary artists, with recordings edited to fit the game's structure. Remix functions let players rearrange musical elements, extending the idea of controlling a song beyond a scored performance. Multiplayer adds another way to divide attention across its tracks. Directed by Greg LoPiccolo, FreQuency established the musical interaction that Harmonix developed in Amplitude in 2003. Its focus on bringing individual parts into a mix offered an early expression of the studio's interest in making recorded music something people could play together.
